overview: Goryeo, founded by Wang Geon in 918, ruled a united Korea from 936 and gave the country its name. Its Buddhist court produced jade-green celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana and the first books printed from metal type.

items.text: A ritual text, the Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun, was printed from metal movable type by the record of the time, more than two centuries before Gutenberg; the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way.
The Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist canon in Chinese script, was carved on more than 81,000 wooden blocks between 1236 and 1251 as a prayer for deliverance from the Mongols.
Celadon with a jade-green glaze and inlaid black and white designs reached its height in the twelfth century.
Buddhist paintings on silk, gilt-bronze sculpture and sutras written in gold and silver on indigo paper.
The Tripitaka blocks have been kept at Haeinsa temple since 1398 and can still be printed from after nearly 800 years.
Buddhism was the state faith, with temples, festivals and monks who held rank at court.
Civil service examinations on the Chinese classics and composition began under King Gwangjong, with separate examinations for monks.
The name Korea comes from Goryeo, carried west by merchants and travelers.
Haeinsa's depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana were listed by UNESCO; the celadons are national treasures.

fall.text: General Yi Seong-gye, who had turned his army back from a campaign against Ming in 1388, deposed the last Goryeo king and took the throne in 1392 as the founder of Joseon.

sources.title: Khan Academy and the Asian Art Museum, The Goryeo dynasty (918 to 1392)
